claim: Each increment of reliability can cost far more than the last, up to 100x.
quote: as we build systems, cost does not increase linearly as reliability increments -- an incremental improvement in reliability may cost 100x more than the previous increment.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: Each additional nine is an order of magnitude closer to 100% availability.
quote: Each additional nine corresponds to an order of magnitude improvement toward 100% availability.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: Time-based availability is uptime divided by uptime plus downtime.
quote: availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime)
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)
note: Formula is an image (alt text 'Time-based availability'); transcribed from the image.

claim: Google defines availability as request success rate: successful requests over total requests.
quote: availability = successful requests / total requests
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)
note: Formula is an image (alt text 'Aggregate availability'); transcribed from the image.

claim: Time-based availability is usually not meaningful for globally distributed services, so Google uses request success rate.
quote: instead of using metrics around uptime, we define availability in terms of the request success rate .
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: 2.5 million requests a day at a 99.99% daily target allows 250 errors.
quote: a system that serves 2.5M requests in a day with a daily availability target of 99.99% can serve up to 250 errors and still hit its target for that given day.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: A 99.99% target allows up to 52.56 minutes of downtime a year.
quote: a system with an availability target of 99.99% can be down for up to 52.56 minutes in a year and stay within its availability target
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: Worked example: moving 99.9% to 99.99% on a $1M service is worth $900, so the nine is worth buying only if it costs less.
quote: In this case, if the cost of improving availability by one nine is less than $900, it is worth the investment.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)
note: Inputs listed above it: improvement 99.9% to 99.99%, increase 0.09%, revenue $1M, value $1M * 0.0009 = $900.

claim: Releases continue while error budget remains.
quote: As long as the uptime measured is above the SLO -- in other words, as long as there is error budget remaining -- new releases can be pushed.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: When SLO violations exhaust the budget, releases are temporarily halted.
quote: If SLO violations occur frequently enough to expend the error budget, releases are temporarily halted while additional resources are invested in system testing and development
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: At a 99.999% quarterly SLO, failing 0.0002% of queries spends 20% of the budget.
quote: If a problem causes us to fail 0.0002% of the expected queries for the quarter, the problem spends 20% of the service’s quarterly error budget.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: An error budget aligns incentives between SRE and product development.
quote: An error budget aligns incentives and emphasizes joint ownership between SRE and product development.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 3 Embracing Risk (Marc Alvidrez)

claim: SRE book Appendix A tabulates allowed downtime per year/quarter/month/week/day/hour for 90% to 99.999%; e.g. 99.9% is 8.76 h/yr and 43.2 min/month; 99.99% is 52.6 min/yr and 4.32 min/month; 99.999% is 5.26 min/yr and 25.9 s/month.
quote: Assuming no planned downtime, Table 1-1 indicates how much downtime is permitted to reach a given availability level.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), Appendix A Availability Table

claim: An SLI is a quantitative measure of some aspect of the service level.
quote: An SLI is a service level indicator -- a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI.
quote: An SLO is a service level objective : a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: An SLA is a contract with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing the SLOs.
quote: SLAs are service level agreements : an explicit or implicit contract with your users that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs they contain.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: If missing the target has no explicit consequence, it is an SLO, not an SLA.
quote: ask "what happens if the SLOs aren’t met?": if there is no explicit consequence, then you are almost certainly looking at an SLO.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: Choose just enough SLOs and defend each one.
quote: Choose just enough SLOs to provide good coverage of your system’s attributes. Defend the SLOs you pick: if you can’t ever win a conversation about priorities by quoting a particular SLO, it’s probably not worth having that SLO.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: Google prefers percentiles over the mean because they expose the long tail.
quote: We generally prefer to work with percentiles rather than the mean (arithmetic average) of a set of values. Doing so makes it possible to consider the long tail of data points
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: A simple average can hide tail latency; in Figure 4-1, 5% of requests are 20 times slower than the typical 50 ms.
quote: A simple average can obscure these tail latencies, as well as changes in them. Figure 4-1 provides an example: although a typical request is served in about 50 ms, 5% of requests are 20 times slower!
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)

claim: Keep a tighter internal SLO than the one advertised to users.
quote: Using a tighter internal SLO than the SLO advertised to users gives you room to respond to chronic problems before they become visible externally.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 4 Service Level Objectives (Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith)
note: Under the heading 'Keep a safety margin'.

claim: The workbook recommends the SLI as good events divided by total events.
quote: we generally recommend treating the SLI as the ratio of two numbers: the number of good events divided by the total number of events.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)
note: The chapter says 'total number of events'; the phrase 'valid events' does not appear on this page.

claim: Error budget is 100% minus the SLO; at 99.9% and 3 million requests in four weeks, the budget is 3,000 errors.
quote: the error budget is 100% minus the SLO. For example, if you have a 99.9% success ratio SLO, then a service that receives 3 million requests over a four-week period had a budget of 3,000 (0.1%) errors
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: Request-driven services: availability, latency, quality.
quote: Availability The proportion of requests that resulted in a successful response. ... Latency The proportion of requests that were faster than some threshold.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)
note: Table 2-1. Quality: proportion of responses served in an undegraded state.

claim: Pipelines: freshness, correctness, coverage.
quote: Freshness The proportion of the data that was updated more recently than some time threshold. ... Correctness The proportion of records coming into the pipeline that resulted in the correct value coming out.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)
note: Table 2-1. Coverage: for batch, proportion of jobs that processed above some target amount of data; for streaming, proportion of incoming records successfully processed within some time window.

claim: Storage: durability.
quote: Durability The proportion of records written that can be successfully read.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: Pick five or fewer SLI types.
quote: We recommend choosing a small number (five or fewer) of SLI types that represent the most critical functionality to your customers.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: A four-week rolling window is a good general-purpose interval.
quote: We have found a four-week rolling window to be a good general-purpose interval. We complement this time frame with weekly summaries for task prioritization and quarterly summarized reports for project planning.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: Rolling windows should be an integral number of weeks so each contains the same number of weekends.
quote: We recommend defining this period as an integral number of weeks so it always contains the same number of weekends.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: The chapter points to Appendix B for an example error budget policy.
quote: For an example SLO document and an example error budget policy, see Appendixes Example SLO Document and Example Error Budget Policy .
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: Common policies on exhausting the budget: stop feature launches or move engineering time to reliability.
quote: Common policies include stopping feature launches until the service is once again within SLO or devoting some or all engineering time to working on reliability-related bugs.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 2 Implementing SLOs (Steven Thurgood, David Ferguson)

claim: Burn rate is how fast the service consumes error budget relative to the SLO.
quote: Burn rate is how fast, relative to the SLO, the service consumes the error budget.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: Burn rate 1 uses exactly the whole budget by the end of the window (0.1% errors at 99.9% over 30 days).
quote: With an SLO of 99.9% over a time window of 30 days, a constant 0.1% error rate uses exactly all of the error budget: a burn rate of 1.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: Table 5-4 at 99.9%: burn 1 = 0.1% errors, exhausts in 30 days; 2 = 0.2%, 15 days; 10 = 1%, 3 days; 1,000 = 100%, 43 minutes.
quote: Table 5-4. Burn rates and time to complete budget exhaustion
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)
note: Row values transcribed from the table.

claim: Recommended: page on 2% budget in 1 h (burn 14.4), page on 5% in 6 h (burn 6), ticket on 10% in 3 days (burn 1).
quote: We recommend 2% budget consumption in one hour and 5% budget consumption in six hours as reasonable starting numbers for paging, and 10% budget consumption in three days as a good baseline for ticket alerts.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)
note: Table 5-6 rows: 2% | 1 hour | 14.4 | Page; 5% | 6 hours | 6 | Page; 10% | 3 days | 1 | Ticket.

claim: Table 5-8 (99.9% SLO): Page, long 1 h, short 5 min, burn 14.4, 2%; Page, 6 h, 30 min, 6, 5%; Ticket, 3 days, 6 h, 1, 10%.
quote: We recommend the parameters listed in Table 5-8 as the starting point for your SLO-based alerting configuration.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)
note: Table 5-8 'Recommended parameters for a 99.9% SLO alerting configuration'; rows transcribed from the table.

claim: Short window should be 1/12 of the long window.
quote: A good guideline is to make the short window 1/12 the duration of the long window
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: Example: page when 14.4x burn holds over both the last hour and the last five minutes.
quote: you can send a page-level alert when you exceed the 14.4x burn rate over both the previous one hour and the previous five minutes. This alert fires only once you’ve consumed 2% of the budget
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: Time for a burn-rate alert to fire is (1 - SLO) / error ratio x alerting window size x burn rate; budget consumed at firing is burn rate x window / period.
quote: For burn rate–based alerts, the time taken for an alert to fire is:
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)
note: Formula follows in MathML: ((1 − SLO) / error ratio) × alerting window size × burn rate, transcribed from the MathML. Next formula: error budget consumed = (burn rate × alerting window size) / period.

claim: 5% of a 30-day budget in one hour requires a burn rate of 36.
quote: Five percent of a 30-day error budget spend over one hour requires a burn rate of 36.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: At a 90% target the 2%-in-1h page can never fire, because a total outage burns only 1.4% in an hour.
quote: Because a 100% outage consumes only 1.4% of the budget in that hour, this alert could never fire.
source: Google SRE workbook (Beyer, Murphy, Rensin, Kawahara, Thorne, eds., O'Reilly 2018), ch. 5 Alerting on SLOs (Steven Thurgood)

claim: Google incident management is based on the Incident Command System.
quote: Google’s incident management system is based on the Incident Command System, 79 which is known for its clarity and scalability.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents (Andrew Stribblehill)

claim: Incident Commander holds the high-level state and holds every role not delegated.
quote: The incident commander holds the high-level state about the incident. ... De facto , the commander holds all positions that they have not delegated.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents (Andrew Stribblehill)

claim: The Ops lead's team is the only group modifying the system during an incident.
quote: The operations team should be the only group modifying the system during an incident.
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents (Andrew Stribblehill)

claim: The Communication role is the public face of the response and issues periodic updates.
quote: This person is the public face of the incident response task force. Their duties most definitely include issuing periodic updates to the incident response team and stakeholders (usually via email)
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents (Andrew Stribblehill)

claim: Planning handles longer-term issues: bugs, handoffs, tracking divergence from normal.
quote: The planning role supports Ops by dealing with longer-term issues, such as filing bugs, ordering dinner, arranging handoffs, and tracking how the system has diverged from the norm
source: Google SRE book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents (Andrew Stribblehill)
